Single Number: every element appears twice except one
XOR is commutative and a ^ a = 0, so only the unpaired value is left. O(n) time, O(1) space.
Number of 1 Bits (Hamming weight)
Brian Kernighan's trick loops once per set bit, not once per bit position. It also works for negative numbers, because the loop ends when n becomes 0.
Counting Bits from 0 to n
This is DP on bits. i >> 1 has already been computed, so the whole table takes O(n).
Reverse Bits of a 32-bit integer
Take the lowest bit off n and add it to res, 32 times. Always O(32).
Power of Two
A power of two has exactly one bit set, so clearing its lowest set bit leaves 0. The n > 0 check excludes 0 and Integer.MIN_VALUE. O(1).
Missing Number in 0..n (XOR)
XOR every index with every value. Each number that is present cancels out, which leaves the missing one. O(n) time, O(1) space, and unlike the sum formula it cannot overflow.
Subsets using a bitmask
Each mask from 0 to 2^n − 1 stands for one subset. O(n · 2^n). This only works for small n (about 20 or fewer).
Sum of Two Integers without + or -
XOR adds without carrying, and AND shifted left gives the carry. Repeat until there is no carry left. Two's complement makes this work for negative numbers too. At most 32 iterations.
Single Number II (every other element appears three times)

XOR alone fails because three copies don't cancel. Count each bit position modulo 3: bits from the triples sum to a multiple of 3. O(32·n) time, O(1) space, and it works for negatives because bit 31 is handled too. The compact "ones/twos" state-machine version also exists but is harder to explain.
Single Number III (two numbers appear once, the rest twice)
XOR of everything gives a ^ b. Any set bit in it separates a from b, so partition by that bit and XOR each group to isolate them. O(n) time, O(1) space.
Hamming Distance and Total Hamming Distance
XOR marks the differing bits and Integer.bitCount counts them. For all pairs, counting per bit position turns O(n²) into O(32·n).
Power of Four
A power of four is a power of two whose single bit sits at an even index; the mask 0x55555555 (binary 0101...) selects those positions. Alternative: power of two and n % 3 == 1. O(1).
Gray Code (successive values differ by one bit)

The i-th Gray code is i ^ (i >> 1). Incrementing i flips a run of trailing bits, and the XOR with the shifted value cancels all but one of those flips. O(2ⁿ). The reflect-and-prefix construction is the alternative explanation.
Reverse Integer (return 0 on 32-bit overflow)

Check for overflow before multiplying. The edge case of exactly MAX/10 cannot overflow here because the last digit of a valid 10-digit int is at most 2. In Java, % and / truncate toward zero, so negatives work without special handling. O(log₁₀ n).
Java bit questions: >> vs >>>, two's complement and shift gotchas

Java has no unsigned int type, so >>> is how you treat an int as unsigned when shifting (e.g. counting bits of a negative number, otherwise while (n != 0) n >>= 1 loops forever). Know the Integer helpers: bitCount, highestOneBit, numberOfTrailingZeros, reverse, toBinaryString.
Find the odd one out: XOR vs HashSet vs sum formula

| HashSet / HashMap | Sum formula | XOR all values
Time | O(n) average | O(n) | O(n)
Extra space | O(n) | O(1) | O(1)
Overflow risk | None | Yes for large n or values; use long | None
Works for | Any frequency pattern | Missing Number (0..n) | Pairs cancel: Single Number, Missing Number
Three-times variant (Single Number II) | Works | No | Plain XOR fails; count bits mod 3
Rule of thumb: XOR works because a ^ a = 0 and a ^ 0 = a, in any order. Mention the HashSet first, then XOR as the O(1) space answer.
Counting set bits: Integer.bitCount vs n & (n - 1) loop vs shifting 32 times

| Shift and test each bit | Kernighan: n &= n - 1 | Integer.bitCount
Iterations | 32 (or until n == 0 with >>>) | Number of 1 bits | Constant; usually a single CPU popcount instruction
Negative input | Must use >>> (with >> a negative never reaches 0) | Works | Works
Shows understanding | Basic | Yes, the classic interview answer | Mention as the production choice
Counting bits for 0..n | O(32 n) | O(total set bits) | O(n); DP bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1) also O(n)
Interview tip: write Kernighan's loop, explain that each step removes the lowest set bit, and mention Integer.bitCount.
Generating subsets: bitmask loop vs backtracking

| Bitmask 0 .. 2ⁿ - 1 | Backtracking
Time | O(n · 2ⁿ) | O(n · 2ⁿ)
Recursion | None | Depth n
Size limit | n ≤ 30 with int, 62 with long (in practice n ≤ ~20 anyway) | Same exponential limit
Pruning (stop when sum too big) | Hard | Easy
Skipping duplicates | Awkward | Sort + skip rule
Also used for | DP over subsets (dp[mask]), visited sets in TSP-style BFS | Any constraint search
Rule of thumb: plain "all subsets" → either. Need pruning or duplicate handling → backtracking. Need a compact state key for memoisation → bitmask.
A set of flags: int / long bitmask vs boolean[] vs BitSet

| int / long mask | boolean[] | java.util.BitSet
Capacity | 32 / 64 flags | Any size | Any size, grows
Memory per flag | 1 bit | Usually 1 byte (JVM dependent) | 1 bit (stored in long words)
Usable as a HashMap key / DP index | Yes, it is just a number | No (array identity) | Yes, but heavier
Set operations | &, |, ^ in O(1) | Loop | and(), or(), xor(), cardinality()
Rule of thumb: up to 64 items and you need the state as a key → long mask. Large sieve-style flags → BitSet or boolean[]; boolean[] is simplest to read.
